title: Waking the Goddess Early
hookLine: night six: Bengal wakes the goddess out of season, the way Rama once did
carry: akal bodhan: devotion wakes the goddess
tomorrow: why do the books rest on night seven?

cards: Drums, big ones, slung on the shoulder, and the sound carries down the lane. In Kolkata and across Bengal, around this point in the nights, Durga Puja gets under way.
Inside a decorated tent called a pandal stands a clay goddess with many arms, a lion at her feet and the buffalo demon under her spear, her four children beside her.
And on this sixth evening, before anything else, the priests do something that sounds strange. They wake her up.

teach.b: Where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night belongs to Katyayani, named, the story says, for the sage Katyayana.
In Bengal the sixth evening has its own rite: bodhon, the awakening. Tradition says the gods rest through the southern half of the year, and autumn falls inside it.
The goddess's older, timely worship is in spring; Bengal still keeps it as Basanti Puja.

teach.h: AKAL BODHAN: CALLED OUT OF SEASON.
teach.b: The autumn festival is called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening, and the Bengali Ramayana of Krittivas tells how it began. Rama is about to fight Ravana to bring Sita home, and he needs the goddess now, not in spring.
He gathers a hundred and eight blue lotuses for the offering, and counting them out, he finds one missing. The goddess has hidden it, to test him.
People called Rama lotus-eyed. So he takes up an arrow to offer one of his own eyes in place of the flower. Before he can, she appears, stops his hand, and blesses him to win.
That's the teaching under the drums, and its name is bhakti, devotion, at full strength. The goddess isn't kept by a calendar. She answers a heart that holds nothing back.
So Bengal's festival begins by calling her awake, and at Sandhi Puja, as the eighth day turns into the ninth, a hundred and eight lotuses are offered in memory of Rama's.

Earlier this year you met her as Uma, the daughter coming home. Tonight is how she's called. And that's the comfort for a busy life now: you don't wait for the right season, or the perfect day, to turn to God.
A whole heart is the right time.

how: In Bengal, Durga Puja begins with bodhon, the awakening of the goddess, on the sixth evening; the autumn worship is called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening, after Rama's worship before his battle, and at Sandhi Puja 108 lotuses are offered. Where the nine forms are kept, the sixth night honors Katyayani.

games.why: Rama takes up an arrow to give his eye. the goddess stops his hand and blesses him. she answers devotion that holds nothing back.

practice: Hold a flower if one is near, or cup your empty hands as if you held one, the way people do at pushpanjali, the flower offering at Durga Puja. Bring what Rama brought: not a perfect time, just a whole heart. Then offer it.
If you pray, you can say Om Durgayai namah, salutations to Durga, or use your own words. If you don't, offer the flower to the one thing you most want to give yourself to fully this week.
